turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sean, Mrs Brennan, come on in. How are things with you?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's not grand. He's eighteen and his asthma is at him again, wheezy after a cold.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ah, that's no fun at all. Tell me how it's been, in your own time.

[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He had a cold, the usual, and then the wheeze started. I was going to say a week, but no, it's been two weeks. It comes and goes, and walking or the stairs sets it off.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Two weeks, so. Sean, are you feeling that wheeze yourself?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any cough with it?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Have you felt hot, or had a temperature at all?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): And any phlegm coming up?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0014] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You'll get the one word out of him, doctor. That's just the way he is.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's perfectly alright. How's the tummy been, any upset there?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you still at the college?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke at all?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand. What inhalers have you in the house?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Blue. Brown.
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He mixes the two of them up. I do as well, if I'm honest.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ah sure, loads of people do. The blue one is salbutamol, your reliever, for when the wheeze is at you. The brown one is the preventer, for every day.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often are you using the blue one, Sean?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Maybe five, six times a day. Two puffs.
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The brown preventer is beclomethasone, two hundred micrograms, two puffs twice a day. He skips the morning one.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay. Any allergies I should know about, medicines or anything else?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0032] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Hold on, he got a rash off penicillin when he was small. The old doctor told us to avoid it. He says he doesn't remember.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Don't remember.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll keep penicillin off the list, so, given that story, even if you're not sure of it yourself.
[SEG0035] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry we were a bit late in. The traffic on the M50 was bumper to bumper the whole way.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Was it really? I came in early and the road was empty. Did ye see the hurling on Sunday?
[SEG0037] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We did, over at my sister's. Her little lad was marching around in a jersey three sizes too big.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ah, that's lovely. How old is he now?
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Four. He has the whole house calling him the captain. The weather was gorgeous, not a cloud.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): We had rain here all evening. I was going to cut the grass and I just sat in instead.
[SEG0041] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His uncle was giving out about the referee the whole way home. I nearly fell asleep in the car.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ha, fair play to you for sitting through that. Right so, back to you, Sean.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): How are the nights?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Bad.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): What's happening at night?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Coughing all night. Can't stop. Chest gets tight. Can't lie flat.
[SEG0047] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I can hear that cough from the landing. He told me this morning there was no cough. Teenagers, honestly.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the cough is there, and the chest tightens on you. May I have a listen?
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nice deep breaths. There's a wheeze both sides, louder on the left. No crackles. Your throat looks clear.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. I don't think you need steroid tablets for this. We'll sort the inhalers and leave the tablets out.
[SEG0052] person_4 (NURSE): Sorry to interrupt, I've his peak flow from outside.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're grand, come in. What did you get?

[SEG0054] person_4 (NURSE): The first go was three hundred and ten, he didn't seal the mouthpiece. Done properly it's three hundred and forty litres a minute. Pulse is ninety-two beats a minute, and his oxygen level is ninety-six percent.
[SEG0055] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): When he was well last summer his best was about five hundred and fifty litres a minute.
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ah, three forty is lower than I expected. I'm changing my mind on those tablets.
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): This is a flare of the asthma after the cold. We'll add prednisolone, thirty milligrams... no, forty milligrams by mouth, once a day, for five days.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay.
[SEG0059] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He'll make a face at that. He hates tablets.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Take them with food in the morning, and stop after the five days. Keep the blue one to two puffs when you're wheezy, not all day long if you can help it.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the brown one, two puffs every morning and every night, even on the days you feel grand. Blue when the wheeze hits, brown to keep it away.
[SEG0063] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll mark the boxes so he doesn't mix them up.
[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): That'd be brilliant. If you can't get a full sentence out, or the breathing gets worse, go straight to the emergency department.
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): Right.
[SEG0066] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back here in a week, and we'll check the peak flow again.
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand.
[SEG0068] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thanks, doctor. We'll be in.
[SEG0069] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mind how you go. And good luck to the little captain.

spec.situation: Teenager or adult wheezy after a cold; confuses blue and brown inhaler; uses the reliever 'maybe five, six times a day'; peak flow numbers read by the nurse. Doctor adds a steroid course.
features: denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

bad.reason: Cold is mentioned earlier, but not explicitly stated as resolved.
Patient denies allergies, but family reports penicillin rash and doctor keeps penicillin off list.

omissions.text: Initial denial of cough was recorded incompletely: when first asked about cough, the patient said no, but later clarified he had coughing all night. This contradiction/changed history is not captured as a negative finding or uncertainty.
The nurse reported an initial peak flow of 310 L/min on the first attempt because he did not seal the mouthpiece; only the corrected 340 L/min was recorded.

Doctor initially stated he did not think steroid tablets were needed and then explicitly changed his mind after the peak flow result; this real change in plan/disagreement with the earlier assessment is not recorded.
Plan to recheck the peak flow again at the follow-up visit in one week was stated but not recorded.
